newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Clinton urges Romania to press on to join NATO.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Romania to press on to join NATO.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton urged Romanians on Friday to stick to their dream of joining NATO, saying their country was "one of the strongest candidates" for membership in two years' time.

"I know that Romania would have liked to be among the first of Europe's new democracies to join NATO," Clinton told tens of thousands of people jammed into central Bucharest's University Square in brilliant late afternoon sunshine.

"I welcome Romania's deep desire to contribute even more fully to Europe's security and strength. I want that too -- for Europe, America and you -- and I say to you today: Stay the course and Romania will cross the milestone."

The speech, highlight of an eight-hour stop in Romania, followed talks with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu during which he urged his reformist administration to press on with efforts to introduce economic and political change.

Speaking in University Square, where dozens of students were killed during the 1989 rebellion which toppled communism, Clinton praised reforms launched since centrists defeated leftists in elections last year. He also applauded efforts to mend fences with Romania's neighbours Hungary and Ukraine.
He said no other people had suffered as much as Romanians under communism and that as long as Romania pursued change "America will be by your side."
"The door to NATO is open. It will stay open. And we will help you walk through it," he said. "NATO is committed to review aspiring members in 1999 and Romania is one of the strongest candidates."

Clinton, the first U.S. president to visit Romania in 22 years, had led resistance to a broad initial wave of eastward expansion for NATO. A NATO summit this week in Madrid issued invitations to start talks on membership to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, passing over Romania and Slovenia.
Despite the setback in Madrid, enthusiastic young people in the square shouted "Clinton! Clinton!" and "NATO! NATO!" and waved small Romanian and U.S. flags.
Constantinescu said the Madrid summit had "declared Romania as a privileged partner for the second wave of its expansion provided the economic and political reforms continue".
And he told the crowd: "We are not going to stop because the vast majority of the Romanian people want to live in a stable and prosperous country."

As he approached the rostrum, Clinton stood head bowed near several white stone crosses marking the spot where young protesters were shot dead scant days before Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was executed in December 1989.

After the address, he was handed a Romanian blue yellow and red tricolour with the centre ripped out -- the symbol of the 1989 revolt during which the communist crest was systematically torn from flags.
